name: Capernaum
blurb: Capernaum was a fishing village established during the time of the Hasmoneans in Israel, located on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee. It had a population of about 1,500 in the 1st century AD. Archaeological excavations have revealed two ancient synagogues built successively at the same spot.

imageReview.note: Viewed in full. Depicts no person — stone, inscription, ruin, map or aerial site only.

name: Cyrus Cylinder
blurb: The Cyrus Cylinder is an ancient clay cylinder, now broken into several pieces, on which is written an Achaemenid royal inscription in Akkadian cuneiform script in the name of the Persian king Cyrus the Great. It dates from the 6th century BC and was discovered in the ruins of the ancient Mesopotamian city of Babylon in 1879.

imageReview.note: Viewed in full. Depicts no person — stone, inscription, ruin, map or aerial site only.

name: Dead Sea Scrolls
blurb: The Dead Sea Scrolls (DSS), in the narrow sense identical with the Qumran Caves Scrolls, are a set of ancient Jewish biblical manuscripts from the Second Temple period. They were discovered over a period of ten years, between 1946 and 1956, at the Qumran Caves near Ein Feshkha in the West Bank, on the northern shore of the Dead Sea.

imageReview.note: Viewed in full. Depicts no person — storage jars only, photographed at the Jordan Museum, Amman.

imageAttribution: Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin FRCP(Glasg), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Herodium
blurb: The Herodeion, in Latin: Herodium, in Modern Hebrew: הרודיון Herodion, known in Arabic as Jabal al-Fureidis is a fortified desert palace built by Herod the Great, king of Judaea, in the first century BCE.

imageReview.note: Viewed in full. Depicts no person — stone, inscription, ruin, map or aerial site only.

name: Siloam tunnel
blurb: The newer Siloam Tunnel, also known as Hezekiah's Tunnel, is a water tunnel that was carved within the City of David in ancient times, now located in the Arab neighborhood of Silwan in eastern Jerusalem.

imageReview.note: Viewed in full. Depicts no person — stone, inscription, ruin, map or aerial site only.

name: Jacob's Well
blurb: Jacob's Well, also known as Jacob's Fountain or the Well of Sychar, is a Christian holy site located in Balata village, a suburb of the Palestinian city of Nablus in the West Bank.

imageReview.reviewedBy: Gokul (product owner) — exception approved via Claude Code
imageReview.note: The crypt interior includes framed icons of haloed figures in the background, on the wall behind the well. The subject of the photo is the well itself, not a person; the product owner explicitly approved this specific photo as an exception to "never depict", accepting incidental background icons where the artifact's own subject is not a person. This is a one-off call for this photo, not a change to the standing guardrail.

name: Ketef Hinnom
blurb: Ketef Hinnom is an archaeological site discovered in the 1970s southwest of the Old City of Jerusalem. Archaeological excavations held at the site uncovered a series of Iron Age period Judahite burial chambers, dating to the 7th and 6th centuries BCE.

imageReview.note: Viewed in full. Depicts no person — stone, inscription, ruin, map or aerial site only.

name: Lachish reliefs
blurb: The Lachish reliefs are a set of Assyrian palace reliefs narrating the story of the Assyrian victory over the kingdom of Judah during the siege of Lachish in 701 BC. Carved between 700 and 681 BC, as a decoration of the South-West Palace of Sennacherib in Nineveh, the relief is today in the British Museum in London, and was included as it…

imageReview.note: The relief carving itself depicts human figures in every known photo and is withheld under "never depict". Substituted with an aerial photo of the Tel Lachish site instead — viewed in full, depicts no person.

imageAttribution: Tel Lachish, aerial 01.JPG, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Tel Megiddo
blurb: Tel Megiddo is the site of the ancient city of Megiddo, the remains of which form a tell or archaeological mound, situated in northern Israel at the western edge of the Jezreel Valley. During the Bronze Age, Megiddo was an important Canaanite city-state, and in the Iron Age, it became a royal city in the Kingdom of Israel.

imageReview.note: Viewed in full. Depicts no person — stone, inscription, ruin, map or aerial site only.

name: Merneptah Stele
blurb: The Merneptah Stele, also known as the Israel Stele or the Victory Stele of Merneptah, is an inscription by Merneptah, a pharaoh in ancient Egypt who reigned from 1213 to 1203 BCE. Discovered by Flinders Petrie at Thebes in 1896, it is now housed at the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

imageReview.note: The lunette at the top of the stele is a figural relief depicting persons. Withheld under "never depict".

name: Mesha Stele
blurb: The Mesha Stele, also known as the Moabite Stone, is a stele dated around 840 BCE containing a significant Canaanite inscription in the name of King Mesha of Moab. Mesha tells how Chemosh, the god of Moab, had been angry with his people and had allowed them to be subjugated to the Kingdom of Israel, but at length, Chemosh returned and ass…

name: Pool of Siloam
blurb: The term Pool of Siloam refers to several rock-cut pools located southeast of the walls of the Old City of Jerusalem. The pools were fed by the waters of the Gihon Spring, carried there by the Siloam tunnel.

imageReview.note: Viewed in full. Depicts no person — stone, inscription, ruin, map or aerial site only.

name: Siloam inscription
blurb: The Siloam inscription, Silwan inscription or Shiloah inscription, known as KAI 189, is a Hebrew inscription found in the Siloam tunnel which brings water from the Gihon Spring to the Pool of Siloam, located in the City of David in East Jerusalem neighborhood of Silwan.

imageReview.note: Viewed in full. Depicts no person — stone, inscription, ruin, map or aerial site only.

name: Sennacherib's Annals
blurb: Sennacherib's Annals are the annals of Sennacherib, emperor of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. They are found inscribed on several artifacts, and the final versions were found in three clay prisms inscribed with the same text: the Taylor Prism is in the British Museum, the ISAC or Chicago Prism in the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures…

imageReview.note: Viewed in full. Depicts no person — the inscribed clay prism only.

imageAttribution: Taylor Prism, British Museum.jpg, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Tel Dan stele
blurb: The Tel Dan Stele is a fragmentary stele with an Old Aramaic inscription written in the Phoenician script. It is generally dated to the 9th-century BCE, though some scholars have proposed later dates; it is one of the earliest, extra-biblical references to a Davidic dynasty.

imageReview.note: Viewed in full. Depicts no person — stone, inscription, ruin, map or aerial site only.

name: Western Wall
blurb: The Western Wall is an ancient retaining wall of the built-up hill known to Jews and Christians as the Temple Mount of Jerusalem. Its most famous section, known by the same name, often shortened by Jews to the Kotel or Kosel, is known in the West as the Wailing Wall, and in the Arab world and Islamic world as the Buraq Wall.

imageReview.note: Viewed in full. Depicts no person — close-up of the stone blocks only.
